title: Quantifying training intensity distribution in elite endurance athletes: is there evidence for an "optimal" distribution?
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
population: Eleven nationally competitive male junior cross-country skiers
findings: 384 sessions (347 endurance, 37 strength) over 32 consecutive days; 318 endurance sessions analysed in three zones bounded by VT1 and VT2.
Heart-rate distribution was 75+/-3% / 8+/-3% / 17+/-4% (zones 1/2/3); session-RPE distribution was 76+/-4% / 6+/-5% / 18+/-7%.
Blood lactate over 60 consecutive sessions: 71% at <=2.0 mM, 7% at 2-4 mM, 22% above 4 mM.

Authors describe a polarized pattern (about 75% clearly below, 15-20% substantially above the VT1-VT2 zone) and state that elite endurance athletes train surprisingly little at lactate-threshold intensity.
limitations: Observational, 32 days, 11 male skiers, so it describes what athletes do and does not show the pattern is optimal. Not runners. Counts are by session (endurance sessions), not time.
implications: Use a three-zone model anchored on VT1/LT1 and VT2/LT2 (or equivalent HR/pace anchors) as the engine's internal intensity vocabulary.
Treat about 75-80% low / 15-20% high with a small zone 2 as a prior for high-volume plans, not as proof of optimality.
Session RPE agreed closely with HR-zone analysis in this sample, so session RPE is a reasonable fallback when HR data are missing.

verification.notes: Crossref: title, journal, first author match; published online 2004-10-27, print issue 2006-02, so year 2006 kept (volume year). Every number checked against Europe PMC abstract.
